Title: Easter Malugala's journey to the carrier world
NewsSummary: Easter Mugala joined the first intake of BScN students at AKU-SONAM in Dar es Salaam graduating in 2005
NewsContent:
Easter Malugal graduated with a Diploma in General Nursing and Midwifery from Muhimbili School of Nursing in 1983, and was employed in the government sector for next 2 years. In 2002, she joined the first intake of BScN nurses at AKU-SONAM in Dar es Salaam.

After graduation in 2005, she returned to the Aga Khan Hospital in Dar for one year but in 2007 she joined the Benjamin Mkapa HIV Foundation in Zanzibar where she made considerable contribution in the reduction of maternal and infant mortality rates in Michiweni District on Pemba Island.
 'There was no theatre in the District Hospital, so we took our clients to Chakechake District. The nurses and health care providers caring for the pregnant mothers and newborns had big knowledge gaps in the management of emergencies.' She says. 'They did not know when to refer so I trained them in the main elements of dangerous deliveries. We made sure all nurses became knowledgeable in the signs and symptoms of dangerous labor. Sometimes I assessed the patient myself, and nurses observed me; and the next morning they would practice, while I supervised. This ensures sustainability of care in the labor ward', she adds. 'In Pemba, some of my colleagues didn't know how to apply for further education. I encouraged them and showed them the way.  

One nurse from Michiweni later graduated from AKU'. In 2008, Easter was appointed National Training Coordinator (Malaria program) at World Vision in Dar-es-salaam where she worked for a while before joining the International Centre for AIDS Care and Treatment Programs (ICAP) in 2011. While at ICAP she helped establish the Tanzania Health Promotion Support.  She also served as a Field Officer at Prevention of Mother to Child HIV Transmission Services where she oversaw the availability of HIV related services to coastal communities in Tanzania, building the capacity of health care workers. 
Currently, she is a Health Field Officer at the Walter Reed Foundation, which operates in the southern highlands of Tanzania where she contributing the reduction in HIV related mortality through testing of mothers, fathers and infants
